problems.title: Omegas — original Question 3
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 3. On the petition date, if Omegas held funds subject to Datacomp's state-law right to reclaim those funds via a “constructive trust,” doesn't the bankruptcy estate also succeed to Omegas's interest in those funds under § 541(a)(1) and (d) subject to Datacomp's superior claim to those funds? I.e., even if Datacomp's right to those funds is a “claim” within the meaning of § 101(5)(A), doesn't the state-law constructive trust remedy also give Datacomp a “lien” on those specific funds that must be recognized and adequately protected in the bankruptcy proceedings? See § 101(37). Should it matter whether state law calls Datacomp's claim to the funds a “property interest” or a “remedy”?

problems.title: Omegas — original Question 4
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 4. Isn't the method by which bankruptcy sorts out the competing priority rights of creditors in a debtor's property via § 544(a)(1)? Why didn't the Omegas court ever ask whether a judgment creditor that levied on the funds at issue on the petition date would prevail over Datacomp's constructive trust claim to those funds? What do you think the answer would be? If state law affords constructive trust claims priority over the claims of general unsecured creditors, how are constructive trusts “anathema to the equities of bankruptcy”?

problems.title: Omegas — original Question 5
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 5. The Sixth Circuit emphasized “the Code's placement of the trustee in the position of a first-in-line judgment creditor and bona fide purchaser for value.” Does a trustee have bona fide purchaser powers with respect to personal property, such as the funds at issue in Omegas?

problems.title: Omegas — original Question 6
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 6. If Omegas had stolen the funds at issue from Datacomp and then used those stolen funds to buy Blackacre, Omegas would have a valid state-law constructive trust claim against Blackacre. However, if Omegas sold Blackacre to a bona fide purchaser, for value, without knowledge of Datacomp's unrecorded interest in Blackacre, that purchaser would take Blackacre free and clear of Datacomp's constructive trust claim. Does that mean that unrecorded constructive trust claims against a debtor's real property can be avoided routinely under § 544(a)(3)? Note, that unlike § 544(a)(1), § 544(a)(3) seems to speak only to “any transfer of property of the debtor” and avoidance of “such transfer.” In the case of Datacomp's constructive trust claim against Blackacre, what “transfer of property of the debtor” would a trustee be seeking to avoid?

problems.title: Omegas — original Question 7
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 7. Would the outcome in Omegas be different if a state court had already imposed a constructive trust on the funds at issue prior to Omegas's bankruptcy filing? If a constructive trust is just a “remedy,” why should the timing matter? Aren't substantive rights more important than procedural mechanics? Doesn't bankruptcy itself simply supply a different set of procedural mechanics by which to vindicate parties' underlying substantive rights?

problems.title: Costas — original Question 1
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 1. While it was heartening to see Judge Mills invoke the reasoning of Butner, wouldn't it have been appropriate for him also to assess the impact of Chicago Board of Trade? Can you see why? How might that make a difference? Note the following language in Drye, quoted by Judge Mills: “We look initially to state law to determine what rights the taxpayer has in the property the Government seeks to reach, then to federal law to determine whether the taxpayer's state-delineated rights qualify as ‘property’ or ‘rights to property’ within the compass of the federal tax lien legislation.” If you substitute the words “debtor” for “taxpayer” and “bankruptcy” for “tax lien,” doesn't that describe the Butner-CBOT property regime in bankruptcy?

problems.title: Costas — original Question 4
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt: 4. How would (or should) the case be decided if Dittlof had died within 180 days after Costas filed bankruptcy (see § 541(a)(5)(A)), and Costas then disclaimed? Or if Dittlof had died shortly before Costas filed bankruptcy, Costas filed bankruptcy without having disclaimed, and then Costas disclaimed? Would that be a violation of the automatic stay and an unauthorized post-petition transfer of estate property? If Costas has an “interest in property” within the meaning of Code § 541 in these scenarios, why wouldn't her pre-bankruptcy disclaimer constitute a “mode . . . of disposing of” that very same “interest in property” within the meaning of Code §§ 101(54) & 548(a). If § 541 gives creditors such a “windfall,” why wouldn't § 548 do the same? Is the meaning and scope of “interest of the debtor in property” different as between § 541 and § 548? Should it be?

problems.title: Chomakos — original Question 6
problems.source: User-uploaded Chapter9 original 'Questions' sections (verbatim, never solved)
problems.prompt:
6. From the perspective of an insolvent debtor's creditors, is (a) a 50% chance of receiving $100 equivalent in value to (b) a 100% chance of receiving $50? Was the Sixth Circuit's analysis sensitive to the difference between (a) and (b)?

To see this, assume that Debtor has debts of $12,000 and assets of $10,000. She takes her entire $10,000 in assets and risks it all on a 50-50 bet (a flip of a coin), and the payoff if Debtor wins is $20,000 (i.e., no house advantage). Of course, if she loses the bet, the payoff is zero. Calculate the projected payout — before the coin is flipped — from the perspective of (i) creditors and (ii) Debtor. It might help if you compute the relative economic interests of the creditors and Debtor assuming (i) no bet is ever placed, versus (ii) the bet is placed.
